name: Barito
region: The Barito river basin of southern Borneo, and Madagascar, 7,000 km to the west
defining_innovation: A subgroup of southern Borneo identified by Hudson (1967) from shared sound changes and vocabulary. Its Southeast Barito branch includes both Ma'anyan and Malagasy.

chapters.title: Origins
chapters.body: The Barito languages are spoken along the Barito river and its neighbours in southern Borneo (Indonesian Kalimantan). Ngaju, a regional lingua franca, and Ma'anyan are among the largest. Most are small and have received little attention. One member does not fit the geography at all: **Malagasy**, the national language of Madagascar, off the coast of Africa.

chapters.title: From Borneo to Madagascar
chapters.body:
Early European visitors had already noticed that Malagasy resembled Malay. In 1951 **Otto Christian Dahl**, a Norwegian missionary-linguist, showed that its closest relative is Ma'anyan of southeastern Borneo. The inherited vocabulary is plain once the sound changes are known: Malagasy *maso* 'eye' (`*mata`), *dimy* 'five' (`*lima`), *afo* 'fire' (`*hapuy`).

The crossing of the Indian Ocean probably took place in the second half of the first millennium CE. Adelaar notes that Malagasy has many loanwords from Malay and Javanese, including Sanskrit words that came through Malay. He concludes that the Barito-speaking settlers sailed as part of Malay-led, possibly Srivijayan, voyages. In Madagascar they met Bantu-speaking East Africans, and Malagasy vocabulary and sound structure show that contact, for example *omby* 'cattle', from a Bantu source like Swahili *ng'ombe*.

chapters.title: Writing Malagasy
chapters.body: Malagasy was first written in **Sorabe**, an Arabic-derived script used by scribes in the southeast from about the 15th or 16th century, mostly for religious and astrological texts. In 1823 King Radama I adopted a Latin alphabet devised with missionaries of the London Missionary Society, and a printed Bible, schools and a standard written language based on the Merina dialect followed within a generation.

speakers.note: Almost all are speakers of Malagasy; the Barito languages of southern Borneo have around a million speakers between them.

sources.citation: Eberhard, David M., Gary F. Simons & Charles D. Fennig, eds. 2024. Ethnologue: Languages of the World, 27th ed. Dallas: SIL International.
Rajemisa-Raolison, Régis. 1985. Rakibolana malagasy. Fianarantsoa: Ambozontany.

turning_points.title: Malay and Javanese influence
turning_points.description: Southeast Barito speakers take in Malay and Javanese vocabulary, and through Malay some Sanskrit, before and during the move west. The layer is visible in Malagasy and supports a Malay-led migration.

sources.citation: Adelaar, Alexander & Nikolaus P. Himmelmann, eds. 2005. The Austronesian Languages of Asia and Madagascar. London: Routledge.

turning_points.title: Across the Indian Ocean
turning_points.description: Speakers of a Southeast Barito language settle Madagascar, and Malagasy begins its separate history. The route, the date, and whether the settlement happened in one wave or several are debated. Linguistic, archaeological and genetic estimates do not fully agree.

sources.citation: Dahl, Otto Christian. 1951. Malgache et Maanjan: une comparaison linguistique. Oslo: Egede-Instituttet.
Adelaar, Alexander & Nikolaus P. Himmelmann, eds. 2005. The Austronesian Languages of Asia and Madagascar. London: Routledge.

turning_points.title: Bantu contact in Madagascar
turning_points.description: Intermarriage and trade with Bantu-speaking East Africans bring Bantu vocabulary, especially for animals and farming (*omby* 'cattle'), and may have reinforced Malagasy's tendency for words to end in a vowel.

sources.citation: Adelaar, Alexander & Nikolaus P. Himmelmann, eds. 2005. The Austronesian Languages of Asia and Madagascar. London: Routledge.

turning_points.title: Sorabe: Malagasy in Arabic script
turning_points.description: Scribes in southeastern Madagascar write Malagasy in an adapted Arabic script, mostly for religious and astrological manuscripts. When and how the script arrived is uncertain.

sources.citation: Adelaar, Alexander & Nikolaus P. Himmelmann, eds. 2005. The Austronesian Languages of Asia and Madagascar. London: Routledge.

turning_points.title: Latin alphabet under Radama I
turning_points.description: The Merina king Radama I adopts a Latin orthography developed with London Missionary Society teachers. It remains the basis of written Malagasy today.

sources.citation: Adelaar, Alexander & Nikolaus P. Himmelmann, eds. 2005. The Austronesian Languages of Asia and Madagascar. London: Routledge.

contested_classifications.proposed_grouping: Malagasy as Southeast Barito: Malagasy's closest relatives are Ma'anyan and its neighbours in southern Borneo
contested_classifications.evidence_for: Dahl showed regular sound correspondences and shared innovations between Malagasy and Ma'anyan, and later work confirms that Malagasy groups with Southeast Barito and not with Malay, despite its many Malay loanwords.
contested_classifications.evidence_against: The heavy Malay and Javanese layer in Malagasy once led scholars to link it directly with Malay or other western Indonesian languages. Some still see the settlers as a mixed population, with Barito speech only one part of their background. The genealogical placement is secure, but it does not settle who the settlers were.

sources.citation: Dahl, Otto Christian. 1951. Malgache et Maanjan: une comparaison linguistique. Oslo: Egede-Instituttet.
Hudson, Alfred B. 1967. The Barito Isolects of Borneo. Ithaca: Cornell University Southeast Asia Program.
